output.title: Recovering from partial automation starts with one workflow
output.body:
If you are recovering from partial automation, don’t start with “What AI can we add back?” Start with one workflow that was partly automated and then stalled, broke, or got abandoned. Invoice data entry, lead follow-up, and customer FAQ replies are different problems; mixing them is how small automations turn into maintenance hobbies.

The decision rule is simple: keep investing only if the workflow is repeatable, measurable, and frequent enough to justify the setup work. The 8–10 hours-a-week pain point is only a persona scenario, not a market statistic or a promise. If the underlying process has changed, a broken automation may simply need to stay broken.

Ask one practical question: who approves the output? If the answer is always “me” or “a person,” AI-assisted automation may fit. If the answer is “nobody checks it” or the system would run without review, you need explicit controls before you trust it. Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

Next step: pick one half-broken workflow, write down in two sentences what still happens by hand and where the automation failed, then mark whether the output needs human approval. That is enough to see whether the problem is scope or software. Bareni builds inside the owner’s own tools and accounts, with finished code handed over and accounts kept in the owner’s name from the start; that is policy, not a promise of perfect portability.
